title: Cash In a Value, Burn Its Neighbours
statement:
You have a bag of positive integers nums. You may repeat this move as long as numbers remain: pick any number x from the bag, remove it, and earn x points. At the same time every copy of x − 1 and x + 1 still in the bag is thrown away and earns nothing.

Other copies of x itself stay in the bag and can be cashed in later. Return the largest total you can earn.

examples.why: Cash in all three 3s for 9; that burns the 2s and the 4. Starting with the biggest number (4) burns the 3s and caps you at 4 + 2 + 2 = 8.
Cashing in one 5 burns the 6 but not the other 5s, so all three 5s count.
No two values are next to each other, so nothing ever burns and you keep everything.

hints: If you cash in one copy of x, you might as well cash in every copy. So only the total per value matters.
Add up all copies of each value into gain[v]. Now taking value v forbids v − 1 and v + 1. Where have you seen "pick items, never two neighbours" before?
Walk the values in increasing order with two running totals: best if you take the current value, and best if you skip it. Taking v is allowed only on top of the best total that skipped v − 1.

explain.intuition:
Once you cash in a value, its neighbours are gone for good, and the other copies of that value become free money. So the decision is per value, not per copy: take value v (and earn v × count) or skip it. Taking v rules out v − 1 and v + 1.

Lay the values out on a number line with gain[v] = v × count(v). Now it is the classic "rob houses on a street but never two neighbours" problem: best(v) = max(best(v − 1), best(v − 2) + gain[v]). Either v is skipped, or v is taken on top of the best answer that ends before v − 1.
steps: Build gain[v] = sum of all copies of v, for v from 0 to the maximum value.
Keep prev2 (best up to v − 2) and prev1 (best up to v − 1), both starting at 0.
For each v: cur = max(prev1, prev2 + gain[v]), then shift: prev2 = prev1, prev1 = cur.
pitfalls: Greedy by biggest value or by biggest total. In [2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4], the biggest value is 4 but the right answer skips it.
Thinking a move burns the other copies of x too. Only x − 1 and x + 1 are burned.
Running the neighbour rule on the sorted list of distinct values without checking the gap. If the next distinct value is not v + 1, it is not blocked.

solutions.title: Neighbour-free picks over the value range
solutions.idea: Sum the copies of each value, then run the take-or-skip recurrence across 0 … max.

solutions.title: Sorted distinct values
solutions.idea: Same recurrence, but only over the values that appear. A value blocks the previous one only when they differ by exactly 1.

followups: Values can be as large as 10⁹ but there are only 20 000 numbers. Which of the two solutions still works?
Return which values to cash in, not just the total.
